title: Northstar Retail - POC cost & batching scoping

Share security and SOC2 docs with Maya

action_items: Jared Mills: Send initial cost model spreadsheet (due 2028-03-22)
Priya Anand: Provide recommended batching/caching config and sample nginx/proxy settings (due 2028-03-23)

summary: AE + SE intro. Customer is Northstar Retail exploring a 2-week POC to validate per-token economics and latency under retail peak patterns. Key scoping: success criteria (P95 tail latency, accuracy retention), workload sizing (concurrent sessions, tokens per session), benchmarks (chat, RAG, summarization), batching/caching levers, and hard budget cap. Agreed pilot plan and owners.
transcript:
Meeting header: 2028-03-18 16:00 UTC | Duration: 55m | Attendees: Jared Mills (Redwood AE), Priya Anand (Redwood SE), Maya Thompson (Northstar Head of ML), Carlos Ruiz (Eng Mgr), Sophie Lee (Product), Liam O'Connor (SRE)

[00:00] Jared: Hey everyone, thanks for making time. This is Jared from Redwood, AE, and with me is Priya our SE. Quick agenda — scope the POC, define success criteria, figure out workload size, and map cost estimates and batching knobs. Maya, want to kick us off with the Northstar context?

[00:18] Maya: Yep, thanks Jared. So we're a retail platform, we run chat-assist on site for customers and a back-of-house summarization pipeline. Peak traffic is around Black Friday but, like, smaller bursts daily. We want to validate cost model and make sure latency won't tank the UX. Primary metric is P95 response time under production-like concurrency. Also concerned about token econs because budgets are tight, we have a $25k monthly cap for inference across the features we plan to move to LLMs.

[01:03] Priya: Got it. When you say per-month cap is that for hosted API only or for dedicated capacity too?

[01:12] Maya: Prefer hosted for speed but open to dedicated if the economics are clearly better and we can meet data residency needs. We also need SOC 2 type II and SSO — we'll send a checklist, Sophie will handle product compliance.

[01:35] Jared: Ok, for the POC we normally run three benchmark slices: 1) Live chat replicate (avg 128 tokens generated per reply), 2) Summarization (avg 512 tokens output), 3) RAG search+generate with 2K context tokens. We'll run synthetic traffic to match your concurrency. Carlos, what's your expected RPS during peak and normal?

[02:02] Carlos: Normal day is around 200 RPS for the chat endpoint, peaks hit up to 1.2k RPS for short windows. But our average session length is small; 3–4 messages per session. Token distribution is spiky — some long summaries. I can pull the trace and share.

[02:27] Priya: Perfect. For costing, quick framing: our hosted per-token run rate depends on model family and sequence length. For example, a 7B-family generation path we often price nominally in the call as ~0.0007 USD per generation token and ~0.00008 USD per input token for encoding — but those are ballpark and vary with batching/quantization. For heavy RAG with 2k context it's material. Batching can reduce effective per-token by 20–45% depending on latency elasticity.

[03:05] Sophie: Quick Q — is the per-token number you quoted including the KV cache benefits or without?

[03:11] Priya: That number's without cache. If you have high prefix reuse (search results or repeated prompts), KV/prefix caching can cut token compute by similar magnitude to batching. Example: for product detail pages where prompts are identical except for product id, prefix caching can save ~30% of generation tokens across the fleet.

[03:38] Maya: So practical question — with our $25k cap, can we do both chat and summarization in prod? What's the rough math?

[03:47] Jared: Let's do an off-the-cuff calc on the call: take conservative numbers — 0.0009 per generation token, 0.0001 per input token. Chat path average 128 gen tokens per reply, so ~$0.115 per 1000 requests? Wait, let me compute… (short pause)

[04:20] Jared: Sorry math broken out: 128 tokens * $0.0009 = $0.1152 per response. At 200 RPS sustained that's 200 * 3600 * 24 ~ 17.28M requests/month — that's unrealistic; we'll use concurrent/session model. Better to use requests per day. If you have 200 RPS average during 10 peak hours, numbers get messy. We'll ask Carlos for real daily requests. But rough: 100k chat responses at $0.1152 ~= $11.5k. Summarization at 512 tokens gen => 0.4608 per summary so 10k summaries ~= $4.6k. RAG is the kicker because of long context and retrieval tokens.

[05:12] Carlos: That helps — our current monthly chat volume that we'd move is ~350k responses. Summaries maybe 20k. RAG would be initial 5k queries with plans to scale.

[05:28] Priya: Using those numbers, chat cost ~$40k (350k * 0.1152 = ~40.3k) which is over your $25k cap. But with batching (20% reduction) and prefix caching for repeated product prompts (another 25% effective), you'd be close to the budget. Also, switching to a quantized 7B variant can reduce costs by 30–40% compared to the default 13B profile.

[06:05] Maya: Ok that's the tradeoff we expected. Can Redwood provide concrete batch-size suggestions and an estimate for tail latency impact? Our UX team won't accept P95 > 300ms for chat.

[06:18] Priya: Yes, we'll propose two configurations in the POC: low-latency (batch size 1–4, modest batching, higher cost) targeting P95 <= 220ms; and cost-optimized (batch size up to 16, aggressive batching and KV caching) targeting 20–35% lower per-token cost with P95 maybe 350–450ms. We'll include a third hybrid — prefer low-latency for customer-facing chat and cost-optimized for background summarization.

[06:58] Sophie: For the background jobs we can tolerate higher latency. Also curious about dedicated reserved pool pricing — is there a breakeven point?

[07:08] Jared: Good question. For dedicated reserved we provide committed-GPU pricing. For example, if your steady-state tokens justify a 3–6 month reserved capacity, committed pricing can reduce per-token by ~25% compared to on-demand hosted. We'll model both in the cost spreadsheet: hosted on-demand, hosted with quantized model, and dedicated 1x/2x reserved GPU tiers.

[07:40] Maya: Excellent. On benchmarks — what's the plan for the POC runs and success criteria exactly?

[07:48] Priya: We'll run three benchmark suites: (A) Chat: replay of 10k real queries (or synthetic with same distribution) to measure p50/p95/p99 latency and throughput; (B) Summarization: 5k docs with avg token lengths, measure quality and cost; (C) RAG: 2k queries with retrieval and 2k context tokens to measure end-to-end latency and token usage. Success criteria: P95 chat <= 220ms (low-latency config) OR cost under $25k monthly across combined workload + quality thresholds (ROUGE/embedding-sim threshold for summaries and RAG). We'll include a fallback policy if tail latency spikes.

[08:46] Carlos: We can supply traces and a segment of production logs for replay. We'll need Redwood to validate results in our staging VPC. Also, we need to test SSO and audit logs — who owns that step?

[09:02] Jared: We'll own the bench runs and results summary. For VPC peering and test infra, we'll coordinate with Carlos and Liam. Sophie will get security docs from our compliance team; we have a SOC2 packet and SAML SSO guide. We'll post links in the follow-up note.

[09:21] Maya: Any notes on memory/kv cache warm-up? We worry about cold-starts during sudden peaks.

[09:28] Priya: Yes, KV cache warm-up matters. Our runtime supports prefix warming and hot-starting a subset of keys. For sudden spikes, the first minute may see higher compute. We'll simulate bursty traffic in the benchmark (spikes to 1.2k RPS) to measure cold penalty. Also recommend a small warm standby pool for Black Friday windows.

[09:55] Jared: Ok next practicals — timeline. We propose:
- 2028-03-20: customer provides traces + sample data
- 2028-03-22: Redwood sends initial cost model and pilot plan
- 2028-03-24 to 2028-03-29: Benchmark runs and tuning
- 2028-03-30: Results review and recommendation
Does that timeline fit?

[10:25] Maya: That works. We'll prioritize getting traces before 3/20.

[10:30] Sophie: Quick objection — we have procurement windows and need estimated committed spend if we consider dedicated. Can you give an example committed quote?

[10:39] Jared: We'll include committed quotes. Example: 2x A100 equivalent reserved for 3 months — rough starting price ballpark; we'll put concrete numbers in the spreadsheet but basically if you commit we can lower token rates substantially and offer SLA.

[10:55] Carlos: Technical deep dive: Priya — what's your recommended batcher config for our infra? Are there network/proxy constraints we should know about?

[11:02] Priya: We recommend keeping request size small and using an in-process queuer at the application edge to accumulate ~5–16 requests for 10–30ms window. For chat low-latency use 1–4 batch size. Also, set keep-alive and gRPC streaming enabled to avoid overhead. On network side, ensure 10Gbps egress between app and peered infra, and avoid TLS session re-creation per request — use persistent connections.

[11:36] Liam: We'll check connectivity. Also need to confirm logs: do you emit per-token breakdowns for cost attribution?

[11:44] Priya: Yes, Redwood Console will show per-request token counts, cost breakdown, and per-route latency histograms. We'll add a demo of the console for the results meeting.

[11:58] Maya: Anything else we're missing?

[12:02] Jared: I'll capture action items. We'll attach: cost-model.xlsx (link: https://redwood.example/poc/northstar/cost-model), bench-plan.md, SOC2 packet, and a short runbook for VPC peering. Priya will bring configs.

[12:20] (small cross talk) Carlos: Sounds good. We'll share traces and a service account for access.

[12:26] Jared: Quick recap: get traces by 3/20, Redwood sends cost model on 3/22, bench runs 3/24-3/29, review 3/30. Action items noted. Any final Qs?

[12:40] Maya: No, thanks — excited to see if we can fit into the $25k box.

[12:45] Jared: Great. We'll follow up with the sheet and a calendar invite for the kickoff. Thanks everyone.

[12:52] End of recording

Notes: Transcription has small errors around technical terms (K-V cache sometimes transcribed as "K V cash"), product names. Shared links will be in follow-up.
